article_title: Maximizing Learning Across Investments Recommendations for Funders
citation: Kara Conroy, Kate Place, Greg Chojnacki. (2023). Maximizing Learning Across Investments: Recommendations for Funders. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/maximizing-learning-across-investments-recommendations-for-funders
title: Structure an M&E process that supports cross-grantee learning while balancing funder, grantee, and community priorities
description: The brief's recommendations aim to help funders "structure an M&E process that supports cross-grantee learning while balancing the priorities of the funder, the grantees, and the communities where research will take place." Cross-grantee learning is presented as a design goal for multi-solution portfolios, with community priorities treated as a party whose interests must be balanced, not overridden.
requirements: The M&E process must be structured to support learning across grantees, not only within single grants.
constraints: The process must balance the priorities of the funder, the grantees, and the communities where research will take place.
target_learners: Funders investing in multiple learning solutions at the same time
target_learning_goals: Cross-grantee learning about whether solutions work, for whom, and in what context
examples: The brief positions this balancing principle as the purpose of its recommendation set for funders.
key_sources: Kara Conroy, Kate Place, Greg Chojnacki. (2023). Maximizing Learning Across Investments: Recommendations for Funders. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/maximizing-learning-across-investments-recommendations-for-funders

article_title: Driving Edtech Coherence and Intentionality: Denver Public Schools’ Innovative Procurement Process
citation: Noakes, S., Shell, A., & Karim, S. (2025). Driving Edtech Coherence and Intentionality: Denver Public Schools' Innovative Procurement Process. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/267
title: Cross-department collaborative edtech review team with content-area review teams
description: The pattern organizes edtech approval as a standing collaboration across district departments: four core teams (EdTech, DoTS, Purchasing, and Legal) plus 14 content teams review each tool before approval. The report states "the development work was driven by a cross-functional team that included staff members from DPS' DoTS, legal, purchasing, and curriculum departments." Content teams are trained as reviewers to judge whether a tool benefits instruction in their content area, and the collaborative team meets bi-weekly to iterate on the process and pipeline.
requirements: Requires representatives from multiple district departments with time and capacity to review tools, and training for content-team reviewers.
constraints: The report notes the process was designed to take about five weeks but could extend to months due to vendor back-and-forths and limited staff capacity, and that school staff are not yet part of the review team.
target_learning_goals: Ensuring approved edtech tools are secure, accessible, standards-aligned, and instructionally effective
examples: DPS staff were divided into four core teams and 14 content teams, including Humanities, Math, SEL, ESS, and Library Services, each providing content expertise in reviews.
key_sources: Noakes, S., Shell, A., & Karim, S. (2025). Driving Edtech Coherence and Intentionality: Denver Public Schools' Innovative Procurement Process. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/267

article_title: Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide
citation: Culturally Responsive Assessment Collaborative. (2025, November). Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/276/
title: Four activity categories scaffold CRA learning from reflection to redesign
description: The guide organizes course activities into four categories that progress from self-examination to system redesign: positionality and reflection; understanding the on-the-ground ecosystem of assessment; critically examining and modifying existing assessment tools or systems; and designing a new reality. This sequence lets students first articulate how their own identities and social positions shape assessment work, then map real assessment ecosystems, critique and adapt existing instruments, and finally design culturally responsive assessments. The categories are presented as a flexible structure instructors adapt to their cohort.
requirements: Activities should be adapted to students' methodological orientations and prior exposure to equity frameworks
target_learners: graduate measurement students with varying quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods orientations
target_learning_goals: practice culturally responsive assessment design
develop reflexivity and critical examination of assessment tools
examples: Activity Category 1 is Positionality and Reflection; Activity Category 4 is Designing a New Reality
key_sources: Culturally Responsive Assessment Collaborative. (2025, November). Introduction to Culturally Responsive Assessment: A Graduate Course Design Guide. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/276/

article_title: Using Research in Ed-Tech: What Does Research-based Product Development Mean?
citation: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Evaluate research for consensus, responsible use, setting fit, and quality rather than cherry picking supportive findings
description: When reviewing research, developers should apply four considerations the guide names: whether there is agreement or competing theories, whether the research is used responsibly, in what settings it was conducted, and whether the findings are trustworthy. The guide warns: "Avoid selectively “cherry picking” research findings that say what you want to hear", illustrating with a scenario of twenty rigorous studies favoring one strategy versus two mediocre studies favoring another. It also recommends peer-reviewed journals as reliable sources and notes that laboratory-only findings may not generalize to classrooms or homes.
requirements: Access to education review journals and quality-evaluation resources such as the Harvard Family Research Project's ten tips
constraints: Findings from regimented laboratory environments may not hold in real-world environments such as classrooms or home use by parents
target_learning_goals: critical evaluation of learning research for product decisions
examples: The guide's cherry-picking scenario contrasts twenty rigorous trigonometry studies favoring strategy A with two mediocre studies favoring strategy B
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2015). Using Research in Ed Tech: The what, how, and why of research-based product development. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f25f7b43-06d9-4732-908b-7409f79b0a91

article_title: Integrating AI-Enabled EdTech in PK16 Education: Five Recommendations
citation: Ruiz, P., Peters Hinton, V., Prado, Y., Noakes, S., Liberman, B., Chillmon, C., Van Nostrand, P., Shell, A., Karim, S., Dallas, D., & Zachariah, I. (2025). Integrating AI-enabled edtech in PK16 education: Five recommendations for state and district leaders. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/273
title: Strengthen AI-edtech governance through cross-functional teams rather than a single department
description: The brief recommends that districts create cross-functional adoption teams with clearly defined roles so that AI-enabled edtech purchases meet both technical requirements and instructional goals. It warns that "If adoption decisions are made without input from multiple perspectives, districts risk adopting AI-enabled edtech tools that either go unused, used without fidelity, or expose students and educators to harm." Teams should include technology experts, curriculum leaders, special education staff, assistive technology leaders, procurement directors, and classroom teachers.
requirements: Needs assessments, product certifications, and evidence-based evaluations to guide decisions
Frameworks that account for the unique risks and opportunities of AI-enabled technologies, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework
constraints: AI-enabled edtech tools introduce new risks related to data privacy, output accuracy, bias, and explainability
target_learners: PK16 students in districts and state education agencies
target_learning_goals: Alignment of edtech purchases with learning goals and safety standards
examples: Denver Public Schools used a rubric and cross-functional team; Chicago Public Schools runs a multi-team vendor onboarding and annual attestation process involving legal, edtech, procurement, IT, risk management, and safety teams

title: Tri-level approach: indicators are needed at individual, setting, and system levels
description: A distinctive feature of the CRIS Framework is its premise that student-level outcome indicators alone are insufficient to promote college readiness. Individual-level indicators identify students needing support; setting-level indicators track school resources and opportunities; system-level indicators monitor district policy and funding infrastructure. The document argues that the tri-level perspective posits that "the consideration of context is critical to monitor whether the conditions (i.e., resources, practices, policies) are in place to promote college readiness."
requirements: Setting- and system-level indicators must inform decisionmaking such as resource allocation and policy design
target_learners: high school students, especially those at risk of falling off track for college
target_learning_goals: monitoring conditions that support college readiness
examples: System-level indicators include availability of guidance counselors, professional development for teachers, and resources supporting data generation and use

target_learning_goals: college readiness monitoring and support allocation

title: Six-stage Cycle of Inquiry connecting indicators to supports
description: The Cycle of Inquiry is the process mechanism that connects indicators with supports: identify, plan, implement supports, monitor progress, adjust supports, and analyze results. Districts take stock of student patterns across schools while schools identify their own students relative to target indicators; data collected during the year allow monitoring and adjustment; end-of-year analysis lays groundwork for the following year. The document stresses that data systems must be "organized to provide timely and easily accessible data to schools so they can monitor progress toward goals."

Ongoing process across school years rather than a one-time review

target_learning_goals: college readiness progress monitoring and support matching
examples: In the identify step, schools create lists of students who may require additional monitoring and support; in the analyze step, results are examined with close attention to subgroups' performance

article_title: College Readiness Indicator Systems Framework
citation: Graciela N. Borsato, Jenny Nagaoka, and Ellen Foley. (2013). College Readiness Indicator Systems Framework. Voices in Urban Education, Fall 2013. https://vue.annenberginstitute.org
title: The CRIS framework: a systematic approach to keeping students on track for college readiness
description: The CRIS framework provides "a conceptual foundation for the development and implementation of college readiness indicator systems." It builds on existing early warning systems in three ways: it targets college readiness rather than only graduation and eligibility, it conceptualizes readiness as including "the knowledge, beliefs, and attitudes necessary to access college and be successful once in college," and it distributes responsibility beyond the district to community partners. It was developed with three urban districts and one school support network.
requirements: Districts must link performance information to post-secondary outcomes and foster a culture of data inquiry with capacity among administrators, educators, and community partners
constraints: The work of building such systems in response to new national college readiness expectations is described as still in an early stage
target_learners: high school students, particularly historically underrepresented students
target_learning_goals: college readiness and post-secondary success
examples: CRIS partners worked with Dallas Independent School District, Pittsburgh Public Schools, San Jose Unified School District, and New Visions for Public Schools in New York City

article_title: Advancing Family and Community Engagement: A Regional Collaborative
citation: Region 15 Comprehensive Center. (2022). Advancing Family and Community Engagement: A Regional Collaborative. https://region15cc.org
title: Design cross-state collaboratives to encourage collaboration and knowledge sharing regardless of each state's internal structure
description: Because family and community engagement initiatives are planned and implemented differently across states — coordinated by a single department or in a disbursed environment — the Collaborative's "key objective was to encourage collaboration and knowledge sharing across and within states regardless of each state's structure." Inclusion was embedded in the infrastructure so that fruitful collaboration did not depend on structural uniformity.
requirements: Understanding how and where engagement initiatives are planned and implemented in each state
Inclusion embedded in the collaborative infrastructure
constraints: Addresses variation among state education agency structures for family and community engagement
target_learners: State education agency family and community engagement leaders
target_learning_goals: Cross-state collaboration
Knowledge sharing across differently structured agencies
examples: Designers asked whether activities were coordinated by a single department or created in a disbursed environment, then built collaboration across states regardless of structure

article_title: Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah
citation: Taylor, T., & Bowman, A. (2024). Design and Implementation of the ESSA Resource Allocation Review: Lessons Learned in Utah. Region 15 Comprehensive Center, WestEd. https://web.stanford.edu/~mshanks/MichaelShanks/files/509554.pdf
title: Bring together a cross-department state team to design and deliver a resource allocation review.
description: The report's first lesson is that a state education agency should assemble staff from many departments to design and deliver the RAR, including the offices of the superintendent, student support services, teaching and learning, special education, state and federal programs, educator effectiveness, financial operations, assessment and accountability, and information technology. The authors argue that "Leveraging the perspectives of multiple departments in the design process enables the state education agency (SEA) to engage in a way that encourages creativity and shared responsibility," producing more effective resource allocation and support for schools.
requirements: The team should encompass key departments including superintendent, student support services, teaching and learning, special education, state and federal programs, educator effectiveness, financial operations, assessment and accountability, and information technology.
target_learning_goals: designing and implementing an equitable resource allocation review process
examples: The report recommends tips such as using existing state-level academic, engagement, and financial data, connecting reporting requirements like the statewide comprehensive needs assessment and IDEA indicators, and leveraging Comprehensive Centers and other experts to guide design.

article_title: Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics
citation: Rebecca Colina Neri, Jahneille Cunningham, and Carlos Sandoval. (2024). Reframing Outcomes of Culturally Responsive and Sustaining Education in Mathematics. WestEd brief.
title: A taxonomy of seven broad outcomes for culturally responsive and sustaining mathematics education
description: The brief organizes CRSE mathematics implementation around a set of outcomes beyond achievement: "students' development of mathematical identity, practice, and empowerment," plus co-construction of knowledge, broadened participation, competent doing, community and family alignment, critical consciousness and cultural competence, and mathematical talk. Table 1 pairs each outcome with a description and a potential classroom measure, positioning these outcomes as "critical drivers of mathematical competence and success" that systems should institutionalize alongside dominant outcomes.

constraints: The brief notes these outcomes are not typically prioritized at scale in large educational systems

target_learning_goals: mathematical identity development
participation in mathematical discourse
competent doing of mathematics
critical consciousness and cultural competence

article_title: Highly Mobile Youth: How State Policy and Local Implementation Can Work Together to Support Youth
citation: Harrington, H., Willis, J., Bishop, J. P., & Cazares-Minero, M. (2026). Highly mobile youth: How state policy and local implementation can work together to support youth. WestEd; Center for the Transformation of Schools, UCLA. https://www.wested.org
title: Cross-sector collaboration framework for supporting highly mobile youth
description: The report defines cross-sector work as "the process by which agencies/organizations across two or more areas of focus—such as education, housing, and so on—share information, resources, and activities to advance shared goals or a unified vision." It uses a framework of cross-sector collaboration with dimensions of aligned supports, monitoring and accountability, and prevention as the coding structure for interviews and policy documents. Aligned systems are argued to improve service delivery, maximize limited resources, and shift practice from reactive to preventative.
requirements: Requires coordination across education, child welfare, housing, and juvenile justice systems that are otherwise largely siloed
constraints: Public policy often prioritizes compliance within individual sectors at the expense of whole-child approaches, per the report
target_learners: Highly mobile youth: students experiencing homelessness, in foster care, classified as migrant, and/or involved with the juvenile justice system
target_learning_goals: Educational continuity and stability
School attendance, grade-level promotion, and graduation
examples: Interviews were thematically coded using the framework of aligned supports, monitoring and accountability, and prevention; policy documents were coded for eligibility criteria and the same alignment dimensions

article_title: Next Generation Science Standards in Practice: Tools and Processes Used by the California NGSS Early Implementers
citation: Tyler, B., & DiRanna, K. (2018). Next Generation Science Standards in practice: Tools and processes used by the California NGSS Early Implementers. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Criteria for Choosing Phenomena tool with anchoring and investigative phenomena categories
description: The Initiative defines phenomena as "occurrences in the natural and human-made world that can be observed and cause one to wonder and ask questions" and distinguishes two types by scale: anchoring phenomena, which are "larger in scale and are the focus of instructional units (i.e., instruction over multiple weeks)", and investigative phenomena, which serve as foci of multi-day learning sequences. The tool provides guiding questions for instructors choosing phenomena, developed in collaboration with #ProjectPhenomena and the San Diego County Office of Education.
requirements: Phenomena must be selected to match target learning outcomes and spark curiosity, taking into account local context, student ability levels, interests, and previous experiences
constraints: The NGSS do not specify which phenomena to use because phenomena need to be relevant to the students in each community
target_learners: K-8 students in participating California districts
target_learning_goals: Three-dimensional NGSS science understanding: explaining phenomena using SEPs, DCIs, and CCCs
examples: Guiding questions include whether students can observe or investigate the phenomenon firsthand or through someone else's experiences, whether explanations would be grade-level appropriate, and whether the phenomenon is relevant to real-world issues or the students' local environment

citation: Browning, A., Kaminsky, C., & Gerzon, N. (2022). Moving toward instructional coherence: How four popular student-centered approaches deepen identity, agency, equity, and community. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Culturally responsive and sustaining education as asset-based use of student cultural identities in learning and curriculum codesign
description: The paper presents CRSE as an approach advancing educational equity by creating culturally affirming and inclusive learning environments. It states that 'Culturally responsive pedagogy uses diverse cultural knowledge, experiences, frames of reference, and methods of expression to make learning engaging, relevant, and effective for students from a range of cultural backgrounds (Gay, 2010).' Culturally sustaining practice additionally sustains evolving student cultures and has the explicit goal of supporting multilingualism and multiculturalism. Students and communities act as codesigners of curriculum, and students are empowered as agents of social change.

Educators value all racial, linguistic, and cultural identities and use them as vehicles of learning
constraints: CRSE supports cultural pluralism, not cultural assimilation
target_learners: K-12 students from a range of cultural backgrounds, including historically marginalized students
target_learning_goals: Positive racial, ethnic, and cultural identity development
recognizing and critiquing social inequalities
academic achievement alongside intellectual and political empowerment

article_title: Community Schools in Rural California: Leveraging Shared Resources in West Kern County
citation: Hernández, L., & Germain, E. (2026). Community schools in rural California: Leveraging shared resources in West Kern County. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/643.620
title: Small rural districts should pool resources through cross-district consortiums to attain capacity no single district could achieve alone
description: The report's first lesson is "Working Stronger Together": by bringing together small, rural districts, the consortium "amassed and leveraged resources that individual districts likely would not have attained by working independently." article_title: Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review
citation: Abramson SL, Sora-Cardenas J, Nandakumar P, Bruce JE, Gopinath N, Zangari LG and Feijóo-García PG (2026). Trust and interaction design in AI-enabled systems: a systematic literature review. Front. Psychol. 17:1932655. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1932655
title: Crampton Smith's four-dimensional framework for operationalizing interaction design factors in AI trust research
description: The review operationalizes interaction design factors—defined as "a design element that can be manipulated to shape how users interact with a system"—using Crampton Smith's four dimensions: Semantics (words, language, tone, linguistic framing), Visual representations (typography, iconography, diagrams, visual hierarchy), Physical embodiment (physical objects and spatial configurations), and Time (dynamic evolution of system behavior during interaction). The framework was chosen for its breadth in accommodating novel AI interaction paradigms, and the nine emergent design factors are interpreted as recurring manifestations within these dimensions rather than an alternative taxonomy.
requirements: Studies must examine how a design-related characteristic of the AI-enabled system or interaction influences trust for a factor to fall within this framework's scope as applied by the review.
constraints: The review notes Nielsen's taxonomy does not treat time as a manipulable design variable, whereas Crampton Smith's inclusion of time is particularly relevant for AI-enabled systems whose outputs may evolve adaptively.
target_learners: users of AI-enabled systems across domains such as healthcare, banking, and education
target_learning_goals: calibrated and appropriate trust in AI-enabled systems

It rests on the assumption that critical incidents are events holding significant potential for gaining insight into error-prone aspects of a work context. A two-phase design is proposed: first identifying critical incidents, possibly with ambulatory assessment methods such as photo elicitation, then semi-structured interviews about the personal theories and knowledge that guided action.

article_title: Beyond the Turk: Alternative platforms for crowdsourcing behavioral research
citation: Eyal Peer, Laura Brandimarte, Sonam Samat, & Alessandro Acquisti. (2016). Beyond the Turk: Alternative platforms for crowdsourcing behavioral research. https://osf.io/murdt
title: A five-measure framework for evaluating crowdsourcing research platforms over time
description: The article proposes a reusable evaluation framework for comparing online participant-recruitment platforms along multiple dimensions of data quality and population characteristics. In its own words, "This framework, which includes measures of attention, reliability, reproducibility, naivety and dishonesty, could also be used to evaluate new platforms that may arise in the future". Each measure is operationalized with a concrete task: attention-check questions, internal reliability (Cronbach's alpha), replication of known effects, self-reported familiarity with common research materials, and an incentive-compatible die-roll cheating task. The authors apply it to MTurk, CrowdFlower, Prolific Academic, and a university participant pool, and show it can track platforms over time after events such as pricing changes.

constraints: The article notes the roots and causes of the differences found between the platforms remain unclear, since participants could only be sampled and not allocated across platforms

target_learning_goals: selecting and evaluating online participant-recruitment platforms for experimental and survey research
examples: In Study 1, 831 participants across CF, ProA, CBDR, and MTurk completed scales, four JDM tasks, attention checks, naivety probes, and a die-roll task under a common one-week recruitment window

citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Critical Decision Method (CDM): four-sweep retrospective interview technique
description: CDM is a narrative-based, retrospective interview technique in which experts reflect on a challenging incident in a complex work domain, seeking to identify knowledge requirements, expertise, and goal structures. It proceeds through four sweeps: incident identification with an uninterrupted narrative walkthrough, timeline verification via incident retelling, deepening probes using prepared cognitive probes about cues, goals, options, and uncertainties, and "What if?" probes that generate hypothetical and practical recommendations. Findings can be presented as visual models of core themes or detailed process pathways over time.

Interviewers familiar with the domain's terminology and work processes
constraints: Pairing with observations and document analysis is not always possible if the decision-making environment is particularly sensitive

target_learning_goals: Unpacking the cognitive processes supporting critical decision-making
examples: Power and Alison (2017) used CDM with emergency responders; Power et al. (2018) used it with ICU referral decisions

article_title: Learning styles concepts and evidence
citation: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2009). Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, Volume 9 Number 3. https://journals.sagepub.com/
title: Crossover-interaction criteria framework for validating learning-styles interventions
description: The review defines a four-part experimental design that any credible validation of learning-styles-based instruction must satisfy: learners are classified by learning style, randomly assigned to at least two instructional methods, all take the same achievement test, and results must show a crossover interaction such that "the learning method that optimizes test performance of one learning-style group is different than the learning method that optimizes the test performance of a second learning-style group." The framework distinguishes acceptable evidence (Figs. 1A–1C) from interactions that look like crossovers only when method is plotted on the horizontal axis. It also separates the broad learning-styles hypothesis from the specific meshing hypothesis.
requirements: Studies must classify learners by style measure, randomly assign within style groups to multiple methods, and give all subjects the same achievement test
constraints: A crossover with instructional method on the horizontal axis does not validate the hypothesis; the style variable must be on the horizontal axis
The framework requires only the crossover interaction, not that the optimal method match each group's style (the meshing hypothesis)
target_learning_goals: Matching instructional presentation format to learners' assessed learning style
examples: Figures 1A–1C illustrate acceptable crossover patterns; Figures 1D–1I and Figure 2 show statistically significant interactions that still provide no support because one method optimizes performance for all learners

citation: Lebuda, I., Hofer, G., & Benedek, M. (2025). Determinants of creative metacognitive monitoring: creativity, personality, and task-related predictors of self-assessed ideas and creative performance. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09432-2
title: Three-level framework of creative metacognitive monitoring (task, performance, response)
description: The article builds on a recently proposed framework of creative metacognition in which monitoring occurs pre-, during, and post-task at three levels of granularity. As printed: "metacognitive monitoring at the task level involves assessing in-real time the characteristics of the task, such as its familiarity, difficulty, or creative demands", while performance-level monitoring evaluates one's creative performance and response-level monitoring evaluates the creative quality of one's own ideas. The performance and response levels correspond to global and local monitoring, and the study uses them to evaluate the framework empirically.
requirements: Distinguishing judgments at performance level (global) from response level (local) requires separate measures of self-assessed performance and self-assessed idea creativity, as the study operationalized them.
constraints: The study focuses solely on self-assessing creative process outcomes (response and performance levels); the task level was not measured.
target_learners: University students and adults performing creative (divergent thinking) tasks
target_learning_goals: Accurate self-assessment of one's creative performance and of the creative quality of one's own ideas
examples: The study measured performance-level monitoring via two self-judgment items after divergent thinking tasks and response-level monitoring via self-ratings of up to ten of one's own ideas, comparing each against external ratings.

article_title: The effects of meta-creative pedagogy on elementary school students’ creative thinking
citation: Nurit Paz-Baruch, Guy Grovas, Zemira R. Mevarech. (2025). The effects of meta-creative pedagogy on elementary school students' creative thinking. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09412-6
title: CREATE: a six-strategy meta-creative pedagogy for fostering creative thinking
description: CREATE is an explicit, theory-grounded meta-creative pedagogy whose acronym names six strategies: comprehending the core problem and subproblems, reconstructing connections, exploring and experimenting, adding more ideas, thinking over constraints and reservations ("True but…"), and evaluating. It combines regulation of cognition, creative self-regulation, and metacognitive pedagogy, training students "to be aware of their creative thinking process, while also fostering fluency, flexibility, and the generation of original ideas." The article presents it as suitable for natural classroom settings.
requirements: Explicit instruction with clear, specific guidance on approaching tasks creatively
Tasks that are complex, unfamiliar, and non-routine (CUN tasks) so meta-creative strategies are needed
constraints: The article reports the flexibility component responded less to the pedagogy on the immediate assessment
target_learning_goals: creative thinking: fluency, flexibility, and originality of ideas
meta-creative self-regulation during creative problem-solving
examples: In the study, teachers introduced CREATE through a Valentine's Day mug-design task, gave students index cards bearing the six strategies, and led reflection on how CREATE helped them think of more and different ideas over about two months of science lessons

article_title: “Valued” Thinking in Education: Liberating the Narrative
citation: Murphy, P. Karen, Ogata, Tyler, & Schoute, Eric C. (2023). “Valued” thinking in education: Liberating the narrative. Educational Psychology Review, 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09754-0
title: Critical pragmatism: experience and discourse as ways of coming to know and verifying knowledge
description: Critical pragmatism is the second liberating theoretical perspective the article overviews. The article states: "Critical pragmatism draws on critical theory as well as pragmatism to emphasize the importance of experience and discourse as ways of coming to know and verifying knowledge." Like standpoint epistemology, it underscores the ways that the social and political realms bear on meaning making, and it centers concrete problems and community-based validation of interpretations.

constraints: The article presents it as a forward-looking theoretical perspective, not a tested instructional model
target_learning_goals: verifying knowledge through experience and discourse rather than narrow epistemic criteria

article_title: Two decades of research on children's creativity development during primary education in relation to task characteristics
citation: O.T.A. Potters, T.J.P. van Schijndel, S. Jak, J. Voogt. (2023). Two decades of research on children's creativity development during primary education in relation to task characteristics. Educational Research Review. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100532
title: A taxonomy of creativity tasks differentiating open- versus close-ended and integrating versus fragmenting tasks
description: The review introduces a taxonomy for mapping creativity tasks used in primary education research. It is "based on a broad conceptualization of creativity, and differentiates between open- and close-ended, and integrating and fragmenting creativity tasks", producing quadrants such as the open-ended fragmenting quadrant. The review also analyzes tasks by the domains of the stimulus and response. The taxonomy is offered as useful for clarifying discussions in creativity research and for designing creativity activities in educational practice.
requirements: Tasks must be classifiable on the two dimensions of open- versus close-ended and integrating versus fragmenting, and can additionally be characterized by stimulus and response domain.
target_learning_goals: creativity development
examples: The review used the taxonomy to classify the tasks in 52 studies, finding open-ended integrating and open-ended fragmenting tasks were frequently used.

article_title: Change and transmission of students' and teachers’ lesson-specific emotions
citation: Sorkkila, M., Malmberg, L.-E., Pöysä, S., Kiuru, N., Lerkkanen, M.-K., & Pakarinen, E. (2026). Change and transmission of students' and teachers' lesson-specific emotions. Learning and Instruction, 102, Article 102298. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102298
title: Cross-directional lesson-specific emotion transmission between teachers and students as an extension of contagion and shared-emotional-experience accounts
description: The article proposes that emotional spirals between teachers and students are cross-directional rather than symmetric: teachers' negative emotions lower students' positive emotions, and students' positive emotions lower teachers' negative emotions. It contributes to "the previous theories of emotion contagion and shared emotional experience" a "novel perspective of cross-directional transmission of positive and negative emotions between teachers and students." Because positive and negative emotions were not shared as prior theories would expect, the article concludes "emotional transmission can be more complex and multifaceted phenomenon, which depends on the roles and relationships between individuals."
requirements: Examining teachers' and students' emotions together in the same lessons, since the article notes it may be more fruitful to investigate them together than separately
constraints: The article notes contagion or desire for similar emotional experiences did not take place between students and teachers as prior theories would expect, possibly because these theories apply particularly to peer networks
The terms predict or transmit do not refer to causality
target_learning_goals: Understanding and supporting classroom emotional dynamics and wellbeing
examples: The article illustrates the spiral with a teacher excited about a topic raising student excitement, students asking more questions, and teacher excitement increasing further

article_title: A group scale of intelligence for use in the first three grades.
citation: Pressey, L. W. (1919). A Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in the First Three Grades. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org
title: Cross-out principle: one uniform minimal response across all tests of a young-child scale
description: A design pattern in which every test in a battery uses the same simple marking response so that clerical labor, fatigue, and confusion between tests are minimized. The article says "In each test he merely crosses out -- using any kind of a mark -- a certain object, part or dot." and notes "By basing all four tests on this same " cross-out" principle the clerical labor of the child in taking the examination, is practically nil." Because responses are uniform, the whole examination of 100 items takes under twenty-five minutes, with children working only three minutes per test.
requirements: Any mark on approximately the right spot is accepted, so no fine eye-hand coordination is demanded
Item material must not require reading or writing
constraints: The author acknowledges simplifying procedure may have left out elements of difficulty, such as the ability to shift from one test to the next
target_learning_goals: Reliable group assessment of general intelligence
examples: Test I asks children to cross out the extra dot; Test II the thing different from the other two in a square; Test III the block left over; Test IV the part of the picture that is wrong

citation: Pressey, S. L. (1920). A Brief Group Scale of Intelligence for Use in School Surveys. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://psycnet.apa.org/journal/edu
title: Grade and age norms for the Cross-out scale based on about 4,000 cases
description: First norms for the final form of the scale: median scores for each of the four tests by grade (3 through 12) and by age (9 through 18), derived from surveys of three Indiana cities totalling "about 4,000 cases" across three revisions. Grade norms are accompanied by median ages so schools with different age-grade distributions can be compared fairly by adjusting scores by half the inter-age interval.

target_learning_goals: interpreting survey scores against grade and age standards

article_title: Understanding mechanisms of generalization following locomotor adaptation
citation: Cristina Rossi, Ryan T. Roemmich & Amy J. Bastian. (2024). Understanding mechanisms of generalization following locomotor adaptation. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00258-2
title: Credit assignment framework: adaptation recalibrates a shared body model that generalizes across contexts and a treadmill-specific model that does not
description: The article proposes that during split-belt adaptation the nervous system updates two distinct forward models: a shared model representing "the general movement dynamics of our body" that generalizes to overground walking, and a treadmill-specific model that does not. Partial generalization arises because only the shared portion of recalibration transfers, producing "a predeﬁned portion of forward model recalibration that generalizes across context". The framework was tested against the slow switching hypothesis using repeated context switching with sensory prediction error eliminated.
requirements: A context switch after overground washout with sensory prediction error eliminated during treadmill blocks to test model predictions
constraints: The authors note this interpretation of speed effects is speculative and that alternative candidate frameworks exist in which internal models are reused and optimized to be shared for different functions
target_learners: healthy adults adapting walking on a split-belt treadmill
target_learning_goals: motor adaptation and generalization of learned walking patterns across contexts
examples: Participants repeatedly switched between treadmill and overground contexts with extended speed match tasks; aftereffects appeared only in the first overground block

article_title: Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders
citation: Katherine L. Jones, Mei Zhou and Dhanisha J. Jhaveri. (2022). Dissecting the role of adult hippocampal neurogenesis towards resilience versus susceptibility to stress-related mood disorders. npj Science of Learning 7:16. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-022-00133-y
title: Critical-period properties hypothesis: immature adult-born neuron excitability and connectivity link chronic stress to mood behaviour
description: The review's working hypothesis is that "the unique properties of adult-born hippocampal neurons during their critical period of maturation are functionally important and causally link chronic stress to altered mood-related behaviour". It posits that chronic stress alters the cellular and physiological properties of these neurons and their pattern of connectivity, producing a dysfunctional hippocampal circuit, and that antidepressants act in part by modulating distinct properties of immature adult-born neurons. Immature neurons exhibit "a critical period of heightened intrinsic excitability and synaptic plasticity" at approximately 4–6 weeks of neuron age, giving them capacity to influence dentate gyrus circuit activity and behaviour.
requirements: Future studies must monitor and manipulate stress-induced changes in molecular, cellular and physiological properties of adult-born neurons, map their connectome, and use spatially and temporally controlled manipulations during behavioural tasks
constraints: The hypothesis is a proposal for future work, not a tested result; prior evidence rests on manipulations with off-target effects and brain-wide ablation that preclude determining the precise role of adult-born hippocampal neurons
target_learners: rodent models in translational neuropsychiatric research
target_learning_goals: understanding mechanisms linking stress-induced changes in adult hippocampal neurogenesis to affective behaviour
examples: The review proposes two posits: chronic stress alters properties and connectivity of immature adult-born neurons, and antidepressants modulate distinct properties of these immature neurons

citation: Heffernan, N. T., Ostrow, K. S., Kelly, K., Selent, D., Van Inwegen, E. G., Xiong, X., & Williams, J. J. (2016). The Future of Adaptive Learning: Does the Crowd Hold the Key? Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:615–644. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-016-0094-z

citation: Khachatryan, G. A., Romashov, A. V., Khachatryan, A. R., Gaudino, S. J., Khachatryan, J. M., Guarian, K. R., & Yufa, N. V. (2014). title: Design intelligent tutoring systems for cross-cultural transfer by knowledge-engineering expert teachers from the source tradition
description: The article proposes a methodology for developing intelligent tutoring systems that transfer curriculum between countries: interview a panel of expert teachers from the source tradition, codify their practices into system algorithms and detailed scripts, iteratively pilot in destination-country classrooms, and use the system to deliver instructional experiences directly to students while scaffolding destination teachers' learning. citation: Andrea Horbach, Joey Pehlke, Ronja Laarmann-Quante, Yuning Ding. (2024). Crosslingual Content Scoring in Five Languages Using Machine-Translation and Multilingual Transformer Models. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00370-1
title: Do not use crosslingual automated content scoring for high-stakes assessment at present
description: The article's ethical considerations argue that crosslingual scoring exposes learners to different model biases depending on their answer language, since "learners will be scored by different models depending on their choice of language and thus be subjected to different model biases". Translating all answers into one language is suggested as more advisable, but the article cautions that machine translation quality varies by source language and that multilingual transformer models work differently well for different languages and combinations. It therefore concludes crosslingual scoring is not currently suitable for high-stakes assessment.

constraints: The article states crosslingual scoring is at the moment not suitable for high-stakes assessment

target_learning_goals: fair automated scoring of content in short written answers
examples: The article recommends automatic translation of all learner answers into the same language in which a model has been trained as a more advisable scenario, while noting its caveat about minority-language quality

scientific reasoning and hypothesis testing

article_title: Power Analysis for Cross Level Mediation in CRTs
citation: Ben Kelcey. (2014). Power Analysis for Cross Level Mediation in CRTs. SREE Spring 2014 Conference Abstract.
title: A power-analysis framework for cross-level (3-2-1) mediation in three-level CRTs based on the product of paths a and b with Delta-method variance
description: The article presents a framework in which mediation in a three-level CRT is formulated in a linear structural equation system, and "the mediation effect is the product of the direct effect of the treatment of interest on the mediator (a in expression (1)) by the direct effect of the mediator on the outcome controlling for the treatment (b in expression (2))". The asymptotic variance of the product is estimated with the Delta method following Sobel, and the resulting test statistic is used to estimate the power of a given design given a priori estimates of variance components and path coefficients. The framework is applied to plan studies of whether teacher knowledge mediates professional development effects on student achievement.
requirements: A priori estimates of the standardized variance components and the expected magnitude of the path coefficients, as the article states these are needed to estimate the power of a given design
A fully balanced design with equal allocation of school treatment and control conditions, as assumed in the derivations
constraints: The framework assumes linearity, large sample approximations, sequential ignorability, that mediation is not moderated, mediator slopes do not randomly vary across schools, and it does not include latent variables
The mediator-outcome path may be confounded because levels of the mediator were not randomly assigned
target_learners: education researchers designing cluster randomized trials of professional development programs
target_learning_goals: planning adequately powered studies of how teacher-focused interventions affect student achievement through mediators
examples: The article's example design: a professional development program assigned at random to intact schools, hypothesized to increase teachers' pedagogical content knowledge, which in turn increases students' achievement levels

title: Concrete–representational–abstract instructional strategy (CRAIS): a three-stage sequence from concrete materials through drawings to symbols
description: CRAIS is an instructional strategy in which each mathematics concept is taught in three sequenced stages: modelling with concrete materials, then semi-concrete drawings representing concrete objects, then symbolic notation using "only numbers, notation, and mathematical symbols". Each part builds on the previous instruction to promote learning, retention, and conceptual knowledge (Access Center, 2004). The article applies CRAIS to circles, volume of solids, and angles of elevation and depression, involving students in cutting, modelling, and drawing before symbolic representation. Its root is traced to Dale's Cone of Experience, where learners retain more by what they do.
requirements: Teachers should make sure students understand what has been taught at each step before moving instruction to the next stage (NCTM recommendation cited from Berkas & Pattison, 2007)
constraints: The article describes CRAIS as originally a strategy for teaching mathematics to students with learning difficulties (Butler et al., 2003)
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of mathematics topics
achievement in mathematics
examples: In the study, twelve teachers were trained with CRAIS and two delivered the six-week experimental treatment using instructional packages based on the Access Center (2004) steps.

description: The CREDE framework is a constructivist, socio-cultural pedagogical system of five interrelated standards: joint productive activity, language and literacy development, contextualization, teaching complex thinking, and teaching through instructional conversations. citation: Tulin KARACA, Ozlem KORAY. (2017). The Effect of Using the Creative Reversal Act in Science Education on Middle School Students’ Creativity Levels. Eurasian Journal of Educational Research 67 (2017) 199-214. http://dx.doi.org/10.14689/ejer.2017.67.12

description: The article grounds the CRE program in humanism and constructivism. constraints: The article presents this as the design rationale for the CREs, not as a tested mechanism; the study measures perceived SDL competency, not the theory directly
target_learners: first-year medical students (adult learners in pre-clerkship training)
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning
critical reflection
problem-centered integration of knowledge
examples: CRE Part 1 presents unfolding clinical cases with no pre-work, Part 2 is entirely self-directed research of an individually identified learning need, and Part 3 closes with student presentations and verbal formative feedback

title: Critical life events framework: stress theory versus development theory perspectives on transitions
description: The article frames grade retention and repetition as non-normative transitions that can be perceived as critical events, defined as events that trigger profound emotions and stress and require adaptation. It draws on two competing theoretical perspectives: the cognitive-transactional stress theory of Lazarus and Folkman, in which the interplay of event and subjective evaluation determines whether stress arises, and development theory, which emphasizes the potential for change from which people can benefit. The article applies this framework to interpret why well-being trajectories around retention differ across individuals, genders and school types.
requirements: Critical events are defined by the article as events that "trigger profound emotions and stress" and require adaptation, with outcomes depending on individuals' coping resources
constraints: The article states critical events do not necessarily have negative consequences; outcomes depend on individuals' coping resources and the cause, magnitude and relevance of the event
target_learning_goals: well-being during educational transitions and adaptation to non-normative school transitions
examples: The study operationalizes the retention decision year and subsequent repetition year as event-centered time dummies against a baseline of up to 7 years before the decision
key_sources: Rathmann Katharina, Loter Katharina, Vockert Theres. (2020). Critical Events throughout the Educational Career: The Effect of Grade Retention and Repetition on School-Aged Children's Well-Being. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph17114012

article_title: Peer Teaching Increases Knowledge and Changes Perceptions about Genetically Modified Crops in Non-Science Major Undergraduates.

title: Cross-age peer-teaching service-learning program with a repeated genetics/GMO lesson for high school students
description: A 3-week service-learning program in a nonmajors biology course in which undergraduates first master an active-learning lesson on plant biology, genetics, and crop improvement, then teach it to high school students in pairs. The lesson uses "card sorting, card matching, extracting DNA from tomatoes, and completing Punnett squares," framed around drought and crop improvement. Repeated teaching across two weeks was a central feature.
requirements: Undergraduates are trained in the lesson by faculty using question-and-answer modeling and practice with lab partners
Teaching occurs in pairs leading small groups of six to 10 high school students
The same lesson is taught repeatedly across two sequential weeks
constraints: All undergraduates participated as a course requirement, so the study used pre/post assessment rather than control groups
Lesson content and materials are tied to state standards for high school genetics and biotechnology
target_learning_goals: genetics and plant biology concepts
crop improvement through traditional breeding and genetic engineering
informed opinions about GMOs in agriculture
examples: In Fall 2016, 49 students enrolled; pairs of undergraduates taught groups of six to 10 high school students over two weeks, with faculty accompanying them to maintain small group sizes

article_title: Can I Have Your Recipe? Using a Fidelity of Implementation (FOI) Framework to Identify the Key Ingredients of Formative Assessment for Learning.
citation: Offerdahl E. G., McConnell M., Boyer J. (2018). Can I Have Your Recipe? Using a Fidelity of Implementation (FOI) Framework to Identify the Key Ingredients of Formative Assessment for Learning. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.18-02-0029
title: Twelve proposed critical components of formative assessment, organized as structural and instructional groups
description: Applying FOI, the authors propose twelve critical components of formative assessment in two categories: structural (learning objectives, formative assessment prompts, evidence of student understanding, feedback, skills for self-regulated learning, personal pedagogical content knowledge, prior knowledge) and instructional (reveal student understanding, personal pedagogical knowledge and skills, diagnosis of in-progress learning, generate feedback, recognize and respond to feedback). The structural group reflects composition and organization of the intervention; the instructional group reflects "how instructors and students behave and interact with one another." The set is a hypothesis for iterative refinement, not a validated measure.
requirements: Iterative refinement through identifying productive and unproductive adaptations and developing valid and reliable measures of each component
constraints: The proposed components should be viewed as a starting point for measuring the FOI of formative assessment; the level of empirical evidence for each varies, though each has substantial theoretical support
target_learning_goals: Monitoring and supporting progress toward desired learning outcomes through diagnosis and feedback
examples: The article's Table 2 lists each component with a description, e.g., feedback as "a comparison of the learner's current state with the criteria for success" used to generate timely, relevant, actionable feedback

article_title: Teaching anatomy using an active and engaging learning strategy.
citation: Singh K, Bharatha A, Sa B, Adams OP, Majumder MAA. (2019). Teaching anatomy using an active and engaging learning strategy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1590-2
title: Use student-created creative presentations (poems, stories, songs, skits) to teach anatomy actively
description: The active and engaging learning strategy shifts teaching "from knowledge transmission to knowledge construction by students": each student creates a peer-facing presentation of assigned muscles (attachments, actions, blood and nerve supply, clinical anatomy) in a self-chosen creative mode, scored with a rubric for creativity, relevance, accuracy, completeness and confidence. In this study it was embedded in course grading (presentations and spotters each worth 5%).
requirements: Time allocated within the course schedule for preparation and presentation sessions
A scoring rubric covering creativity, relevance, accuracy, completeness and confidence
Baseline and post-presentation spotter assessments to track learning
constraints: Effectiveness of individual presentation modes was not evaluated
Small single-campus sample; authors advise caution generalizing to other settings
Marks may have been influenced by other teaching strategies or prior knowledge
target_learning_goals: Musculoskeletal (limb muscle) anatomy: attachments, actions, blood and nerve supply, applied/clinical anatomy
examples: Students created UL and LL muscle presentations in week 8 and week 11 using poems (37.1%), stories (21.2%), songs (11.4%) and skits (10.6%), each limited to 5 minutes and scored against a ten-mark rubric

article_title: Creative teaching behaviors of health care school teachers in Taiwan: mediating and moderating effects.
citation: Liu Hsing-Yuan, Wang I-Teng. (2019). Creative teaching behaviors of health care school teachers in Taiwan: mediating and moderating effects. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1641-8
title: Mediation and moderation conceptual framework of creative teaching behavior
description: The article proposes a dual-path conceptual framework in which school creative climate (SCC) influences creative teaching behaviors (CTB) through creative teaching self-efficacy (CTS) as mediator, based on Bandura's theory of self-efficacy, and in which school creative climate moderates the association between creative teaching ability and creative teaching behaviors, based on Litwin and Stringer's creative climate model. The authors state they "examined whether creative teaching self-efficacy (CTS) would have a mediating effect (partially or fully) on the relationship between school creative climate (SCC) and creative teaching behaviors (CTB)". Empirical data from the 53-teacher survey confirmed both models.
requirements: Measurement of school creative climate, creative teaching self-efficacy, creative teaching ability, and creative teaching behaviors via validated self-report scales (SCCS, SECTS, CTETITS, CTBS)
constraints: Tested only in a cross-sectional sample of 53 health care school teachers in Taiwan, which the authors state limits generalizability to health care teachers outside Taiwan
target_learners: Health care school teachers in vocational and technical schools (nursing, gerontological care and management, nutrition and health departments)
target_learning_goals: Fostering creativity and creative teaching behaviors in health care education, including developing innovative healthcare products
examples: The authors tested the framework with Pearson correlations, stepwise linear regression, and hierarchical multiple regression on survey data collected October 2016 to January 2017.

article_title: Just watching is not enough: Fostering simulation-based learning with collaboration scripts.
citation: Zottmann Jan M., Dieckmann Peter, Taraszow Tatjana, Rall Marcus, Fischer Frank. (2018). Just watching is not enough: Fostering simulation-based learning with collaboration scripts. GMS Journal for Medical Education 35(3), Doc35. http://www.egms.de/en/journals/zma/2018-35/zma001181.shtml
title: Collaboration script intervention for observational phases of simulation-based emergency courses
description: A concrete collaboration script used in four simulation-based emergency courses: each scripted student observed the simulator team "on the basis of a single CRM principle" and took notes, working in dyads with one "analyst for positive situations" and one "analyst for negative situations". Dyads then jointly selected one successful and one less successful implementation example, and learners switched roles after each scenario to enable perspective change and deeper elaboration.
requirements: Observational phases of about 20 minutes followed by 5-minute collaboration phases in dyads; a one-hour lecture on CRM heuristics during the course
constraints: The script was applied to only some parts of the training, which the authors name as a possible reason for the missing effect on learning outcomes
target_learners: medical students in their 7th to 12th semester
target_learning_goals: application of Crisis Resource Management heuristics in emergency situations
examples: Two courses used the script and two served as controls; the control condition received only a sheet reading "Observe your fellow students in the simulator. You may take notes on this sheet"

article_title: Filling the Gap: Simulation-based Crisis Resource Management Training for Emergency Medicine Residents.
citation: Parsons Jessica R. MD, MSMS; Crichlow Amanda MD, MSMS; Ponnuru Srikala MD; Shewokis Patricia A. PhD; Goswami Varsha MD; Griswold Sharon MD, MPH. (2018). Filling the Gap: Simulation-based Crisis Resource Management Training for Emergency Medicine Residents. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2017.10.35284
title: Simulation-based CRM course for novice EM residents: introductory lecture plus six high-fidelity scenarios with structured debriefs
description: A CRM course consisting of "1) an introductory lecture presentation, and 2) a series of six specialized simulation scenarios." The 30-minute lecture introduces CRM concepts and defines terms such as "closed loop communication," "shared mental model," "workload management," and "situational awareness." Each 10–15 minute scenario is followed by a 30-minute debrief by a single facilitator, using a standardized patient actor or SimMan3G simulator, with cases drawn from the department's existing case bank and modified to meet learning objectives.
requirements: A simulation room, a single simulation debriefing facilitator, and minimal other staff or faculty to serve as confederates in the scenarios
A validated CRM rating scale (Ottawa GRS) and two raters to evaluate team performance
constraints: The CRM principles introduced and evaluated reflect just a subset of those CRM skills needed for EM
Designed for novice EM residents in a two-week introduction-to-residency curriculum
target_learning_goals: Crisis resource management skills: leadership, problem solving, situational awareness, resource utilization, and communication
examples: Fourteen EM interns were randomly divided into four teams, redistributed three times over the course; each intern participated in three cases and observed three additional cases

article_title: Describing complex clinical scenarios at the bed-side: Is a systems science approach useful? Exploring a novel diagrammatic approach to facilitate clinical reasoning.
citation: Jayasinghe S. (2016). Describing complex clinical scenarios at the bed-side: Is a systems science approach useful? Exploring a novel diagrammatic approach to facilitate clinical reasoning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0787-x
title: CRM's educational basis in meaningful learning, cognitive theory of multimedia learning, and Kolb's experiential learning cycle
description: The author argues CRM's theoretical basis broadly fits constructivism and explains its utility through three named theories. Meaningful learning explains why learners found CRM helpful, since "the ability of CRM to link a collection of clinical events adds meaning by relating new information to those already known to the learner". Its combination of words linked by diagrammatic conventions reflects multimedia learning principles, where "words and pictures together" help produce logical mental constructs promoting deeper learning than words alone. CRM also enables reflection and abstract conceptualization, components of Kolb's experiential learning cycle.
requirements: The theoretical account presupposes learners relate mapped clinical events to knowledge they already possess
constraints: The article states further studies are required to explore CRM's utility in retaining such meaningful information in long-term memory
target_learning_goals: understanding complex clinical scenarios
deeper learning through integrated words and pictures
reflective practice
examples: Students drawing CRMs after a presentation, then discussing them in groups, mapping onto the experiential learning cycle

article_title: Certainty rating in pre-and post-tests of study modules in an online clinical pharmacy course - A pilot study to evaluate teaching and learning.
citation: Luetsch Karen, Burrows Judith. (2016). Certainty rating in pre-and post-tests of study modules in an online clinical pharmacy course - A pilot study to evaluate teaching and learning. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0783-1
title: Certainty-rated multiple choice questions (CRMCQs) with four-point certainty scale in formative pre/post-module testing
description: CRMCQs are MCQs to which students add a certainty rating on a four-point Likert scale (no idea/uncertain/certain/very certain), adapted from certainty-based marking studies. In this pilot, sets of 10 case-based or knowledge MCQs per module were administered before and after five study modules of an online postgraduate pharmacotherapeutics course, yielding 1315 matched answer-certainty pairs analysed with paired t-tests and a coding scheme. The element served both learner self-assessment and evaluation of teaching and question design.
requirements: Students instructed how to calibrate 'certain' versus 'very certain' (more than 90% sure for very certain); tests available for a limited time period within the virtual learning environment
constraints: Pilot conducted in a single postgraduate pharmacy course with a small, predominantly female sample; results did not contribute to course marks
target_learning_goals: formative self-assessment
clinical pharmacotherapy knowledge
reflection on certainty of knowledge
examples: Certainty categories were converted to numerical values (1 = no idea to 4 = very certain) and analysed in Excel and R 3.3.1

article_title: Testing CREATE at Community Colleges: An Examination of Faculty Perspectives and Diverse Student Gains.
citation: Kenyon Kristy L., Onorato Morgan E., Gottesman Alan J., Hoque Jamila, Hoskins Sally G. (2016). Testing CREATE at Community Colleges: An Examination of Faculty Perspectives and Diverse Student Gains. CBE—Life Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1187/cbe.15-07-0146
title: CREATE pedagogy: intensive analysis of primary scientific literature using a toolkit of concept mapping, cartooning, figure annotation, data templates, grant panels, and author emails
description: CREATE (Consider, Read, Elucidate hypotheses, Analyze and interpret the data, Think of the next Experiment) is described as "an innovative strategy for teaching and learning in STEM disciplines" in which faculty redesign courses around primary scientific literature rather than a textbook-prescribed curriculum. Its toolkit includes concept mapping, cartooning, annotating/transforming figures and tables, analyzing data with templates, a grant panel activity, and email surveys of paper authors. The email component aims to humanize scientists and "demystif[y] journal articles."
requirements: Faculty redesign their existing courses around primary or other scientific literature using CREATE strategies
A 4.5-d intensive CREATE faculty workshop prepared implementers to use the strategy in their first attempt
constraints: Concerns raised by implementers included content coverage, finding appropriate articles, and student preparation for class activities
On one campus the PIs judged CREATE tools were not applied sufficiently and consistently enough to count as a CREATE course
target_learners: community college (2-yr) students, including majors and nonmajors
target_learning_goals: experimental design ability
critical thinking and data analysis
understanding of the process of science and epistemological beliefs about science
examples: Students concept mapped article paragraphs, cartooned how studies were carried out, annotated figures, designed follow-up experiments reviewed in mock grant panels, and emailed paper authors

article_title: High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for teaching medical students in Brazil about pediatric emergencies.
citation: Couto Thomaz Bittencourt I, Farhat Sylvia C.L., Geis Gary L, Olsen Orjan, Schvartsman Claudio. (2015). High-fidelity simulation versus case-based discussion for teaching medical students in Brazil about pediatric emergencies. Clinics. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4462571/
title: Crossover simulation/case-discussion intervention with pre-, post- and retention MCQ testing
description: An instructional design in which two pediatric emergency themes (anaphylaxis in a teenager, SVT in an infant) were crossed over across two student groups, so each group experienced one high-fidelity simulation and one case-based discussion on the same scenarios. The design was "based on Chiniara's framework for instructional design in simulation and Cook's levels of instructional design", with identical scenario content, images and ancillary exam results across methods, and knowledge measured by piloted MCQs at pre-test, post-test and 4–6-month retention.
requirements: Same scenario, case history, physical exam findings, images and ancillary exam results presented in both methods
Questions developed by pediatric emergency physicians blinded to the scenarios and piloted for validity and reliability
constraints: Groups were pre-assigned by convenience and not randomized; participation was voluntary with 33.7% loss to follow-up at retention
target_learners: sixth-year medical students in a pediatrics rotation
target_learning_goals: management of rare, high-acuity pediatric emergencies (anaphylaxis, SVT)
examples: Group 1 experienced SIM-ANA then CD-SVT; group 2 experienced CD-ANA then SIM-SVT, with tests at rotation end and 4–6 months later
key_sources: Couto Thomaz Bittencourt I, Farhat Sylvia C.L., Geis Gary L, Olsen Orjan, Schvartsman Claudio. (2015). article_title: Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine.
citation: Ilic Dragan, Nordin Rusli Bin, Glasziou Paul, Tilson Julie K, Villanueva Elmer. (2014). Development and validation of the ACE tool: assessing medical trainees' competency in evidence based medicine. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-14-114
title: CREATE framework for classifying EBP assessment tools
description: The CREATE framework (Sicily statement) classifies evidence-based practice assessment tools by category (reaction to educational experience, attitudes, self-efficacy, knowledge, skills, behaviours, benefit to patients) and type (self-report, cognitive testing, performance assessment, activity monitoring, patient-oriented outcomes), crossed with the five EBM steps. The article uses it to justify assessing knowledge and skills via performance assessment: "EBM related knowledge and skills are the only assessment categories that are best examined via performance, or cognitive, assessment". It also guides which constructs suit self-report versus observation.
requirements: Assessment categories should be matched to appropriate assessment types per the framework's guidance
constraints: Step 5 (evaluation/reflection) is deemed inappropriate for dichotomous or multiple-choice formats and best measured through open-ended outcome assessment
target_learning_goals: evidence based practice competency assessment across knowledge, skills, attitudes and behaviour
examples: The authors used CREATE to position the ACE tool as satisfying requirements for examining knowledge and skills across EBM steps 1-4

article_title: Support of Study on Engineering Technology from Physics and Mathematics
citation: Djafar K. Mynbaev, Candido Cabo, Roman Ya. Kezerashvili, Janet Liou-Mark. (2008). Support of Study on Engineering Technology from Physics and Mathematics.
title: Cross-referenced e-modules linking engineering-technology, physics, and mathematics courses via hypertext keywords
description: E-modules of courses in mathematics, physics, computer systems technology (CST), and electrical and telecommunications engineering technology (EET) were developed with cross-references between common key terms and definitions. When a keyword such as "resistance" or "linear equation" appears in an engineering-technology module, clicking it links to the corresponding lecture material in physics or mathematics, and physics concepts link to engineering applications such as fiber-optic communications. The authors state that "e-modules of courses have been developed with cross-references between common key terms and definitions," so students reviewing linked material find themselves in "familiar territory."
requirements: Courses must be placed on both an open Web-based system and a closed Blackboard system, with each Web course linked to a corresponding Blackboard course
constraints: At the time of writing, keyword links from CST networking courses to mathematics and physics material were still being identified rather than complete
target_learners: engineering-technology students at an urban minority-serving college
target_learning_goals: transfer of physics and mathematics knowledge to engineering-technology coursework
examples: An EET student studying Ohm's law clicks on "resistance" to reach the physics discussion, and on "linear equation" to reach the mathematics e-module covering material already studied
key_sources: Djafar K. Mynbaev, Candido Cabo, Roman Ya. Kezerashvili, Janet Liou-Mark. (2008). Support of Study on Engineering Technology from Physics and Mathematics. https://arxiv.org/abs/0807.1950
